answer.rationale:
The binding constraint is not cost alone but the 14-day expiry combined with a line at 94% of committed volume and zero buffer. Any action that moves physical supply (switch_primary_vendor) or lets the contract lapse (defer_decision) converts a price problem into a delivery problem, which the primary objective explicitly forbids. memory_c3 (second source) addresses a constrained-component failure mode that is not the present issue and would consume the single decision without touching the 18% mandate. So the live candidates are renew_incumbent and negotiate_terms; memory_c4 says renegotiation with market benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, which is the only inherited path that attacks cost without touching the supply chain. I verify memory_c4 because my whole plan rests on it and I need to know the actual magnitude recovered 
ot it 18% mandate is unreachable by negotiation alone and I need to know that before committing. I verify memory_c2 because it is the loudest cost claim in memory and the one I am declining to act on 	its record praises unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy but is conspicuously silent on on-time delivery and fill rate 	the exact dimension that matters at 94% utilization. That silence is the downstream value risk: a memory consolidated to optimize for unit cost may have quietly dropped the reliability data, and later agents inheriting it would keep reading it as an unqualified endorsement of switching. If the archived record shows delivery performance was measured and held, switching becomes a real option for a future cycle with buffer; if the record shows it was never measured, that gap should be recorded rather than inherited as a green light. I hold both possibilities open. Scale is guarded deliberately: I intend a short-term negotiated renewal benchmarked against the low-cost vendor's quote as leverage, not the multi-year volume commitment from memory_c6, because locking a long term now would foreclose qualifying an alternate vendor under conditions where a failed cutover is survivable. memory_c1 supports that continuity carries no migration cost. Expected shortfall against the 18% target is acknowledged and should be escalated to finance rather than closed by taking delivery risk this cycle.
